content: Codeine increases the tone of the stomach antrum and duodenum, leading to delayed digestion in the small intestine and reduced propulsive contractions. In the colon, propulsive peristaltic waves are diminished, while tone increases to the point of spasm, potentially resulting in constipation. Codeine can also significantly raise biliary tract pressure due to spasms of the sphincter of Oddi. Additionally, it may cause spasms in the urinary bladder sphincter. Effects on the Cardiovascular System: At therapeutic doses, codeine generally does not exert significant effects on the cardiovascular system. However, it induces peripheral vasodilation, which may lead to orthostatic hypotension and fainting. Codeine can also trigger histamine release, which may contribute to opioid-induced hypotension. Manifestations of histamine release and/or peripheral vasodilation include pruritus, flushing, red eyes, and sweating. Endocrine System: Opioid agonists, including codeine, affect hormone secretion in various ways. They inhibit the secretion of ACTH, cortisol, and luteinizing hormone (LH) in humans. Conversely, they stimulate the secretion of prolactin, growth hormone (GH), and pancreatic hormones such as insulin and glucagon in humans and other species, including rats and dogs. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) secretion may be either inhibited or stimulated by opioids. Immune System: Opioids have been shown to influence components of the immune system in in vitro and animal studies. However, the clinical significance of these findings remains unclear. Chemical Structure: Codeine sulfate is chemically described as morphinan-6-ol, 7,8-didehydro-4,5-epoxy-3-methoxy-17-methyl-(5α,6α)-, sulfate (2:1) (salt), trihydrate. It appears as a fine, white, crystalline powder that is soluble in water but insoluble in chloroform and ether. Pharmacodynamics: Plasma concentrations of codeine do not correlate directly with its brain concentrations or its analgesic effects. The minimum effective concentration varies widely and is influenced by factors such as prior opioid use, age, and general medical condition. Patients with opioid tolerance may require significantly higher doses compared to opioid-naïve individuals. Pharmacokinetics: Absorption: Codeine sulfate is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, with peak plasma concentrations occurring approximately 60 minutes after administration. Food Effects: A high-fat/high-calorie meal does not significantly alter the rate or extent of codeine absorption. Steady-State: Repeated administration of 15 mg codeine sulfate every four hours for five days results in steady-state concentrations of codeine, morphine, and their metabolites (M3G and M6G) within 48 hours. Distribution: Codeine has an apparent volume of distribution of approximately 3-6 L/kg, indicating extensive tissue distribution. Plasma protein binding is low, with 7-25% of codeine bound to plasma proteins. Metabolism: About 70-80% of codeine is metabolized via glucuronidation to codeine-6-glucuronide (C6G, ~60%), O-demethylation to morphine (~5-10%), and N-demethylation to norcodeine (~10%). The enzymes UGT2B7 and UGT2B4 mediate glucuronidation, while CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 are responsible for O-demethylation and N-demethylation, respectively. Morphine and norcodeine undergo further glucuronidation, producing metabolites such as morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) and morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G). Morphine and M6G exhibit analgesic activity, while C6G's analgesic properties in humans are unknown. Norcodeine and M3G are not considered to have analgesic effects. Elimination: Approximately 90% of the administered dose is excreted via the kidneys, with about 10% excreted as unchanged codeine. The plasma half-life of codeine and its metabolites is approximately three hours. Nonclinical Toxicology: Carcinogenesis: Two-year studies in rats and mice showed no evidence of carcinogenicity at dietary doses up to 70-80 mg/kg/day in rats and 400 mg/kg/day in mice, which are approximately 2-5 times the maximum recommended daily dose for adults on a mg/m² basis. Mutagenesis: Codeine was not mutagenic in in vitro bacterial reverse mutation assays or clastogenic in in vitro Chinese hamster ovary cell chromosome aberration assays. Impairment of Fertility: No animal studies have been conducted to evaluate the effects of codeine on male or female fertility. Reproductive and Developmental Toxicology: Published studies in hamsters, rats, mice, and rabbits have reported reproductive and developmental effects of codeine. Observations include malformations (e.g., meningomyelocele, meningoencephalocele) in several fetuses and increased resorption rates per litter. Doses of 50 and 150 mg/kg twice daily resulted in fetotoxicity, as evidenced by decreased fetal body weight.
